decks.title: Linear Programming — Part 1: Terms, models and feasible regions
goals: Use the terms decision variable, objective function, constraint and optimisation
State advantages, limitations and application areas of linear programming
Formulate manufacturing, diet and transportation-type problems in two variables
Draw feasible regions and classify them as bounded, unbounded or empty

slides.heading: Linear Programming, Part 1
slides.body_md: Linear programming finds the best plan when limited resources are shared between two activities.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: the vocabulary of linear programming, its uses and limits, the three types of problem, formulating a model, and drawing the feasible region.
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance.

slides.narration: Welcome to linear programming. Every business, kitchen and transport depot shares limited resources between competing activities. In this part we learn the vocabulary, see where the method is used and where it falls short, turn word problems into mathematical models, and draw the region of plans that are actually possible.

slides.heading: The parts of a model
slides.body_md: Decision variables, an objective function, constraints and non-negativity.

rows: Linear quantity to maximise or minimise

visual.alt: Table of terms with meanings and an imagined dairy example: decision variables are the paneer and curd batches; the objective is the profit 3000 x plus 4000 y; the constraints are pasteuriser and packing hours; non-negativity keeps both at least zero; optimisation means finding the most profitable feasible plan.
visual.caption: Every linear programming problem has these parts.

slides.narration: Every model has the same parts. The decision variables are the quantities we are free to choose. The objective function is the linear quantity we want to make as large or as small as possible, such as profit or cost. The constraints are linear limits on the variables, and non-negativity says the quantities cannot be negative.

slides.heading: Advantages and limitations
bullets: But: linearity, exact data and a single objective are assumed

rows: Only one objective at a time
Easy to re-solve when data change
Answers may be fractional for whole items

visual.alt: Two-column table: advantages are best use of scarce resources, clear systematic decisions, showing bottlenecks and spare capacity, and easy re-solving when data change; limitations are the linearity assumption, exact coefficients, a single objective and possibly fractional answers.
visual.caption: Know two of each for a 2-mark question.

slides.narration: Linear programming gives the best use of scarce resources and makes the decision clear and easy to revise. But it assumes that everything is proportional, that every number is known exactly, and that there is only one goal. Answers can also be fractions even when the items are whole.

slides.heading: Quick check: a feasible plan
slides.body_md: Which plan obeys both limits of a stall?
slides.narration: Substitute each plan into both inequalities. A plan is feasible only if it satisfies every one of them.

slides.heading: Three types of problem
slides.body_md: Manufacturing, diet and transportation problems.

rows: How much of each product to make
How much of each food to buy
How much to send on each route

visual.alt: Table of the three types of problem: manufacturing decides how much of each product to make, maximising profit under machine, labour and material limits; diet decides how much of each food to buy, minimising cost while meeting minimum nutrients; transportation decides how much to send on each route, minimising cost while meeting supplies and demands.
visual.caption: The type tells you the direction of most inequalities.

slides.narration: Most school problems are of three types. A manufacturing problem decides how much of each product to make, usually maximising profit under limits that read at most. A diet problem decides how much of each food to buy, minimising cost with requirements that read at least. A transportation problem decides how much to send along each route at the least cost.

slides.heading: How to formulate
slides.body_md: Variables, objective, constraints, non-negativity.

nodes.label: Write the objective with its direction
Turn each limit into an inequality

visual.alt: Flow of formulation steps: name the decision variables, write the objective function and whether to maximise or minimise, turn each limit into a linear inequality, and add the non-negativity conditions.
visual.caption: Four steps of formulation.

slides.narration: To formulate a problem, first name the decision variables with their units. Then write the objective function and say whether to maximise or minimise it. Turn every limit in the story into a linear inequality, and finally add the non-negativity conditions.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a dairy model
slides.body_md: An imagined Anand dairy makes paneer and curd. Formulate the problem.

visual.alt: Data table for the imagined dairy: a paneer batch needs 2 pasteuriser hours and 1 packing hour; a curd batch needs 1 and 2; 14 pasteuriser hours and 13 packing hours are available; profits are 3000 and 4000 rupees per batch.
visual.caption: Read the table column by column into inequalities.

slides.narration: Read the table column by column. A paneer batch uses two pasteuriser hours and a curd batch one, with fourteen available, so two x plus y is at most fourteen. Packing gives x plus two y at most thirteen. The profit is three thousand x plus four thousand y, to be maximised, and neither variable can be negative.

slides.heading: Quick check: the non-negativity name
slides.body_md: Name the conditions that keep quantities from being negative.
slides.narration: What do we call the conditions that x and y are at least zero?

slides.heading: Graphing one inequality
slides.body_md: Draw the line, then test a point such as the origin to choose the side.

visual.alt: The line 3 x plus 4 y equals 24 through (8, 0) and (0, 6). The origin lies below the line and the point (6, 5) above it. Testing the origin gives 0 at least 24, which is false, so the solution set of 3 x plus 4 y at least 24 is the side away from the origin.
visual.caption: Origin test: false, so shade the far side.

slides.narration: Each inequality is a half-plane. Draw its boundary line using the two intercepts. Then test a point not on the line, usually the origin. If the inequality is true there, shade the side containing the origin; if it is false, shade the other side. For three x plus four y at least twenty four, the origin fails.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: corners of a region
slides.body_md: Find the corners of the region $x + y \le 9$, $x + 3y \le 15$, $x, y \ge 0$.
bullets: Origin test: shade towards the origin

rows: Origin test: $0 \le 9$, $0 \le 15$ true, so shade towards the origin

visual.alt: Worked example table: the lines x plus y equals 9 and x plus 3 y equals 15 have intercepts (9, 0), (0, 9) and (15, 0), (0, 5); the origin test is true for both, so shade towards the origin; they meet at (6, 3); the corners are (0, 0), (9, 0), (6, 3) and (0, 5).
visual.caption: Corners come from intercepts and intersections.

slides.narration: Plot both lines from their intercepts. The origin satisfies both, so the region lies towards the origin. Subtracting the equations gives two y equals six, so the lines meet at six, three. With the two axis points, the corners are the origin, nine zero, six three and zero five.

slides.heading: A bounded region
slides.body_md: The feasible region is where all the shaded half-planes overlap.

visual.alt: Two lines in the first quadrant: x plus y equals 9 from (9, 0) to the y-axis at 9, and x plus 3 y equals 15 from the y-axis at 5 to the x-axis at 15. They cross at (6, 3). The feasible region is the quadrilateral with corners (0, 0), (9, 0), (6, 3) and (0, 5), below both lines.
visual.caption: A bounded region with four corners.

slides.narration: Here is the region for that example. It is closed on every side, so it is bounded: it could be drawn inside a circle. Its corners are where two boundary lines meet, including the axes. These corners matter most, as Part two will show.

slides.heading: Three constraints
slides.body_md: With three non-trivial constraints, the region can have up to five corners.

visual.alt: Three lines: x plus y equals 12, 2 x plus y equals 20 and x plus 3 y equals 30. The feasible region below all three is a pentagon with corners (0, 0), (10, 0), (8, 4), (3, 9) and (0, 10).
visual.caption: Three non-trivial constraints: up to five corners.

slides.narration: Your syllabus allows up to three constraints besides non-negativity. This handloom region uses three lines and is a pentagon. To find its corners, intersect each pair of lines and keep only the points that satisfy every constraint.

slides.heading: Quick check: count the corners
slides.body_md: How many vertices does an open-ended nutrient region have?
slides.narration: Find where each pair of lines meets and keep only the points that satisfy all three conditions.

slides.heading: An unbounded region
slides.body_md: "At least" constraints keep points away from the origin and often give an unbounded region.

visual.alt: Two lines: x plus y equals 8 and x plus 3 y equals 12, crossing at (6, 2). The feasible region lies above both lines and stretches without end to the upper right; its corners are (0, 8), (6, 2) and (12, 0).
visual.caption: An unbounded region: it has corners but no outer edge.

slides.narration: When the constraints say at least, the region lies away from the origin and may go on without end. This region has three corners but no outer boundary: it is unbounded. Such regions need extra care when we look for an optimum.

slides.heading: An empty region
slides.body_md: If the half-planes do not overlap, there is no feasible solution.

visual.alt: Two lines: x plus y equals 4 from (4, 0) to (0, 4), and 3 x plus 2 y equals 18 from (6, 0) to (0, 9). Points satisfying the first lie on or below the lower line; points satisfying the second lie on or above the upper line. The two sets do not overlap, so the feasible region is empty.
visual.caption: No common region: the problem is infeasible.

slides.narration: Sometimes the constraints contradict each other. A van carrying at most four crates cannot meet a load requirement of eighteen units when each crate is worth at most three. The two half-planes do not overlap, so the feasible region is empty and the problem has no solution.

slides.heading: Bounded, unbounded or empty
slides.body_md: Classify the region before you look for the optimum.

rows: Fits inside a circle: both maximum and minimum exist
Goes on without end: an optimum may or may not exist
No feasible point: no solution at all

visual.alt: Table of region types: a bounded region such as x plus y at most 9 and x plus 3 y at most 15 fits inside a circle and has both a maximum and a minimum; an unbounded region such as x plus y at least 8 and x plus 3 y at least 12 goes on without end and may or may not have an optimum; an empty region such as x plus y at most 4 with 3 x plus 2 y at least 18 has no feasible point.
visual.caption: Classify the region before you optimise.

slides.narration: So a feasible region is of one of three kinds. A bounded region fits inside a circle. An unbounded region goes on without end. An empty region has no points at all. Classify the region first, because the kind of region decides how we look for the optimum.

slides.heading: Quick check: is it feasible?
slides.body_md: Decide whether a nutrition plan meets all three conditions.
slides.narration: Substitute the plan into each of the three conditions.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Each inequality is a half-plane; the region is their overlap
Regions are bounded, unbounded or empty

visual.alt: Summary flow for Part 1: know the terms, formulate the model, shade each half-plane, and find the corners of the feasible region.
visual.caption: Part 1 in one line.

slides.narration: To sum up. A model has decision variables, an objective function, constraints and non-negativity. Problems are usually of the manufacturing, diet or transportation type. Each inequality is a half-plane; the feasible region is where they all overlap. It is bounded, unbounded or empty.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: State what $x$ and $y$ stand for, with units
Read "at least" as $\ge$ and "at most" as $\le$
Label every line and every corner
Check each corner in all constraints

visual.alt: Exam tips table for Part 1: definitions and advantages earn a mark per point; a formulation earns marks for the variables and objective, the constraints and non-negativity; drawing a region earns marks for the lines, the correct side and the corners; the common slip is reversing at least and at most.
visual.caption: Write the units of every variable.

slides.narration: In the examination, always say what x and y stand for. Read at least as greater than or equal to, and at most as less than or equal to. Label every line and every corner on your graph, and check each corner in all the constraints before you use it.

decks.title: Linear Programming — Part 2: Optimal solutions by the corner point method
goals: Explain why the optimum of a linear objective lies at a corner point
Solve problems by the corner point method
Use the half-plane test on unbounded regions and recognise when no optimum exists

slides.heading: Linear Programming, Part 2
slides.body_md: The best plan is found at a corner of the feasible region.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: bounded regions, the corner point method, unbounded regions and the half-plane test, cases with no optimum, and cases with many optimal solutions.
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. Now that we can draw the feasible region, we look for the best plan in it. A remarkable fact makes this easy: for a linear objective, the best value is found at a corner. We will also see what happens when the region is unbounded, when there is no optimum, and when there are many.

slides.heading: Why corners?
slides.body_md: Lines $ax + by = k$ for different $k$ are parallel; the last point of the region they touch is a corner.

visual.alt: The quadrilateral with corners (0, 0), (9, 0), (6, 3) and (0, 5), with two parallel lines 4 x plus 5 y equals 20 and 4 x plus 5 y equals 39. Sliding the line away from the origin, the last point of the region it touches is the corner (6, 3).
visual.caption: Parallel lines $4x + 5y = k$: the last point touched is a corner.

slides.narration: Draw the lines where the objective takes a fixed value. They are all parallel. As the value increases, the line slides away from the origin. The last point of the region it touches is a corner, here six, three. So for a bounded region we only need to check the corners.

slides.heading: The corner point method
slides.body_md: Bounded: compare corner values. Unbounded: also test the half-plane.

nodes.label: Best corner value is the optimum
Test the open half-plane beyond the best value

visual.alt: Flow of the corner point method: draw the feasible region, list every corner, evaluate Z at each corner; if the region is bounded the best corner value is the optimum; if it is unbounded, test the open half-plane beyond the best value.
visual.caption: The corner point method.

slides.narration: Here is the method. Draw the region and list every corner. Evaluate the objective at each corner. If the region is bounded, the largest and smallest corner values are the maximum and minimum. If it is unbounded, the best corner value still has to pass the half-plane test.

slides.heading: Quick check: a dairy vertex
slides.body_md: Find where two dairy boundary lines meet.
slides.narration: Solve the two equations together by elimination.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a handloom unit
slides.body_md: Maximise $Z = 500x + 300y$ on $x + y \le 12$, $2x + y \le 20$, $x + 3y \le 30$, $x, y \ge 0$.

visual.alt: Corner table for the imagined handloom unit: Z equals 500 x plus 300 y is 0 at (0, 0), 5000 at (10, 0), 5200 at (8, 4), 4200 at (3, 9) and 3000 at (0, 10); the maximum is 5200 at (8, 4).
visual.caption: Eight sarees and four stoles a week.

slides.narration: The region is the pentagon we drew in part one. Evaluating five hundred x plus three hundred y at its five corners gives zero, five thousand, five thousand two hundred, four thousand two hundred and three thousand rupees. The greatest is five thousand two hundred, with eight sarees and four stoles.

slides.heading: Unbounded regions and the half-plane test
slides.body_md: Draw the open half-plane beyond the best corner value; if it misses the region, the value is optimal.

visual.alt: Three lines 2 x plus y equals 10, x plus y equals 7 and x plus 2 y equals 10 bound an unbounded region with corners (0, 10), (3, 4), (4, 3) and (10, 0). The line 5 x plus 4 y equals 31 touches the region only at (3, 4); the open half-plane below it contains no feasible point.
visual.caption: Half-plane test: nothing of the region lies below $5x + 4y = 31$.

slides.narration: On an unbounded region the corner values alone are not enough. Take the best corner value and draw the open half-plane on its better side. For a minimum of five x plus four y with best corner value thirty one, the half-plane five x plus four y less than thirty one has no point of the region, so thirty one is the minimum.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: the canteen diet
slides.body_md: Minimise $Z = 5x + 4y$ on $2x + y \ge 10$, $x + y \ge 7$, $x + 2y \ge 10$, $x, y \ge 0$.

visual.alt: Corner table for the imagined canteen: Z equals 5 x plus 4 y is 40 at (0, 10), 31 at (3, 4), 32 at (4, 3) and 50 at (10, 0); the least value is 31, confirmed by the half-plane test.
visual.caption: Unbounded region: confirm with the half-plane.

slides.narration: The canteen region is unbounded, with four corners. The costs at the corners are forty, thirty one, thirty two and fifty rupees. The least is thirty one. Because the region is unbounded, check the open half-plane below it: it contains no feasible point, so three millet and four pulse packets cost the least.

slides.heading: Quick check: a true or false
slides.body_md: Can an unbounded region have a minimum?
slides.narration: Think of the example we just solved.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: when no maximum exists
slides.body_md: On $x + y \ge 8$, $x + 3y \ge 12$, $x, y \ge 0$, does $Z = x + 2y$ have a maximum?

visual.alt: Table for the unbounded region x plus y at least 8 and x plus 3 y at least 12: Z equals x plus 2 y is 16 at (0, 8), 10 at (6, 2) and 12 at (12, 0), but the feasible point (0, 20) gives 40, more than 16, so there is no maximum.
visual.caption: One feasible point beyond the best corner is enough to prove there is no maximum.

slides.narration: The corner values are sixteen, ten and twelve. But the point zero, twenty is feasible and gives forty, which beats every corner. Moving up the y-axis we can make the objective as large as we like. So this objective has no maximum on the region, although it does have a minimum.

slides.heading: Infinitely many optimal solutions
slides.body_md: If the objective line is parallel to an edge, every point of that edge can be optimal.

visual.alt: The pentagon with corners (0, 0), (10, 0), (8, 4), (3, 9) and (0, 10). The objective line x plus y equals 12 lies along the edge from (8, 4) to (3, 9), so every point of that edge gives the same largest value 12.
visual.caption: The objective line is parallel to an edge: infinitely many optima.

slides.narration: Sometimes the objective line is parallel to an edge of the region. Then the best value is reached at two adjacent corners and at every point between them. For the total number of pieces, x plus y, on the handloom pentagon, both eight, four and three, nine give twelve, and so does every point of the edge.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: many best plans
slides.body_md: Maximise $Z = x + y$ on the handloom pentagon.
bullets: Every point of the edge between them is optimal

visual.alt: Corner table for the imagined handloom unit: Z equals 500 x plus 300 y is 0 at (0, 0), 5000 at (10, 0), 5200 at (8, 4), 4200 at (3, 9) and 3000 at (0, 10); the maximum is 5200 at (8, 4).
visual.caption: Eight sarees and four stoles a week.

slides.narration: Evaluate x plus y at the five corners: zero, ten, twelve, twelve and ten. The best value twelve appears at two adjacent corners, so it appears along the whole edge joining them, for example at five and a half, six and a half. The unit can choose any of these plans.

slides.heading: Quick check: two equal corners
slides.body_md: Find the maximum of an objective that ties at two corners.
slides.narration: Evaluate the objective at all four corners and look for a tie.

slides.heading: A transportation-type region
slides.body_md: Two depots and three sites reduce to two variables and three constraints.

visual.alt: The cement transport region: x at most 50 (vertical line), y at most 70 (horizontal line) and x plus y at most 100. Its corners are (0, 0), (50, 0), (50, 50), (30, 70) and (0, 70).
visual.caption: A transportation-type region in two variables.

slides.narration: In the cement problem, depot P sends x tonnes to site A and y tonnes to site B, and every other shipment follows from the supplies and demands. Requiring each shipment to be non-negative gives three constraints and this five-cornered region. The cost is cheapest at fifty, zero.

slides.heading: All the possible outcomes
slides.body_md: Bounded, unbounded with or without an optimum, empty, or many optima.

rows: Maximum and minimum both exist, at corners
best corner passes the half-plane test
That corner value is the optimum
a feasible point beats the best corner
equal best value at two adjacent corners

visual.alt: Table of the possible outcomes: on a bounded region the maximum and minimum both exist at corners; on an unbounded region the best corner value is the optimum if it passes the half-plane test, and there is no optimum if a feasible point beats it; an empty region has no feasible solution; equal best values at two adjacent corners give infinitely many optimal solutions.
visual.caption: Five outcomes to recognise.

slides.narration: Here are all the outcomes you can meet. A bounded region always has a maximum and a minimum at corners. An unbounded region has an optimum only if the best corner value passes the half-plane test. An empty region has no solution. And equal best values at two adjacent corners give infinitely many solutions.

slides.heading: Quick check: count the optima
slides.body_md: How many plans maximise the total pieces?
slides.narration: Look for two corners with the same best value.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Optimum of a linear $Z$ is at a corner
Ties at adjacent corners: infinitely many optima

nodes.label: State the plan and the value

visual.alt: Summary flow for Part 2: find the corners, evaluate Z at the corners, apply the half-plane test if the region is unbounded, and state the optimal plan with its value.
visual.caption: Part 2 in one line.

slides.narration: To sum up. The optimum of a linear objective lies at a corner of the feasible region. On a bounded region, compare the corner values. On an unbounded region, also apply the half-plane test. And if two adjacent corners tie, every point of the edge between them is optimal.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: State the half-plane test for unbounded regions
Give the answer in the words of the problem
Never assume an optimum exists on an unbounded region

rows: formulation 2, corners 1, values 1, answer in context 1
the half-plane check carries a mark
missing a corner where two slanted lines meet

visual.alt: Exam tips table for Part 2: solving graphically earns marks for the region, the corner values and the optimum; a long word problem earns two marks for formulation and marks for the corners, the values and the answer in context; on an unbounded region the half-plane check carries a mark; the common slip is missing a corner where two slanted lines meet.
visual.caption: Always answer in the words of the problem.

slides.narration: In the examination, always show a table of corner values. For an unbounded region, state the half-plane test in words. Give your final answer in the language of the problem, for example eight sarees and four stoles. And never assume that an optimum exists without checking.

notes.title: Linear Programming — chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. Terms of linear programming
sections.body_md:
A **linear programming problem** asks for the maximum or minimum of a linear function of the decision variables, subject to linear constraints.

- **Decision variables** $x, y$: the quantities to be chosen.
- **Objective function** $Z = ax + by$: profit, cost or time, to be optimised.
- **Constraints**: linear inequalities from the limits of the problem.
- **Non-negativity**: $x \ge 0$, $y \ge 0$.
- **Optimisation**: finding the feasible plan with the best value of $Z$.

key_terms.definition_md: A point satisfying every constraint, including non-negativity.
A feasible solution at which Z takes its best value.

formulas.latex: \text{Optimise } Z = ax + by \ \text{subject to linear constraints},\ x, y \ge 0
formulas.label: General form

rows: Linear quantity to maximise or minimise

visual.alt: Table of terms with meanings and an imagined dairy example: decision variables are the paneer and curd batches; the objective is the profit 3000 x plus 4000 y; the constraints are pasteuriser and packing hours; non-negativity keeps both at least zero; optimisation means finding the most profitable feasible plan.
visual.caption: Every linear programming problem has these parts.

sections.heading: 2. Advantages, limitations and application areas
sections.body_md:
**Advantages:** best use of scarce resources; clear, systematic decisions; shows bottlenecks and spare capacity; easy to re-solve when data change.

**Limitations:** assumes linearity (proportional profit and resource use); all coefficients must be known exactly; one objective at a time; answers may be fractional for whole items.

**Application areas:** production planning in factories, diet and feed mixing, transport of goods from depots to markets, allocation of advertising budgets, investment choices.

key_terms.definition_md: Doubling a variable doubles its contribution to Z and to each constraint.

rows: Only one objective at a time
Easy to re-solve when data change
Answers may be fractional for whole items

sections.heading: 3. Types of problem and formulation
sections.body_md:
- **Manufacturing:** maximise profit; constraints usually "at most" ($\le$) on machine hours, labour and material.
- **Diet:** minimise cost; constraints usually "at least" ($\ge$) on nutrients.
- **Transportation-type:** minimise transport cost; express every route through two variables using supplies and demands, then require each amount to be non-negative.

**Steps:** name the variables with units; write $Z$ and its direction; turn each limit into an inequality; add $x, y \ge 0$.

Choosing amounts to send along routes to meet demands at least cost.

sections.heading: 4. Graphing the feasible region
sections.body_md:
Each inequality $ax + by \le c$ (or $\ge c$) is a half-plane bounded by the line $ax + by = c$. Draw the line from its intercepts, then test a point not on it (usually the origin) to choose the side.

The **feasible region** is the common part of all the half-planes in the first quadrant. Its **corner points** are intersections of pairs of boundary lines (including the axes) that satisfy every constraint.

The region may be **bounded**, **unbounded** or **empty**. The ISC course uses at most three constraints besides non-negativity, so a region has at most five corners.

key_terms.definition_md: A vertex of the feasible region: the meeting point of two boundary lines.
A feasible region that cannot be enclosed in a circle.
A problem whose feasible region is empty.

visual.alt: Two lines in the first quadrant: x plus y equals 9 from (9, 0) to the y-axis at 9, and x plus 3 y equals 15 from the y-axis at 5 to the x-axis at 15. They cross at (6, 3). The feasible region is the quadrilateral with corners (0, 0), (9, 0), (6, 3) and (0, 5), below both lines.
visual.caption: A bounded region with four corners.

visuals.alt: The line 3 x plus 4 y equals 24 through (8, 0) and (0, 6). The origin lies below the line and the point (6, 5) above it. Testing the origin gives 0 at least 24, which is false, so the solution set of 3 x plus 4 y at least 24 is the side away from the origin.
visuals.caption: Origin test: false, so shade the far side.

visuals.alt: Three lines: x plus y equals 12, 2 x plus y equals 20 and x plus 3 y equals 30. The feasible region below all three is a pentagon with corners (0, 0), (10, 0), (8, 4), (3, 9) and (0, 10).
visuals.caption: Three non-trivial constraints: up to five corners.

sections.heading: 5. The corner point method
sections.body_md:
**Corner point theorem.** If the feasible region is bounded and non-empty, $Z = ax + by$ has both a maximum and a minimum, each at a corner point.

**Method:** find every corner; evaluate $Z$ at each; the largest and smallest values are the maximum and minimum.

**Unbounded regions:** let $M$ be the best corner value. For a maximum, if the open half-plane $ax + by > M$ has no point in common with the region, $M$ is the maximum; otherwise there is no maximum. (For a minimum use $ax + by < M$.)

key_terms.definition_md: Checking whether the open half-plane beyond the best corner value meets an unbounded region.

formulas.latex: \max Z \text{ on an unbounded region exists} \iff \{ax + by > M\} \cap R = \varnothing
formulas.label: Half-plane test

nodes.label: Best corner value is the optimum
Test the open half-plane beyond the best value

sections.heading: 6. Special cases
sections.body_md:
- **No optimum:** on an unbounded region, a feasible point that beats the best corner value shows that the optimum does not exist in that direction (for example $Z = x + 2y$ on $x + y \ge 8$, $x + 3y \ge 12$ has no maximum).
- **Infeasible:** an empty region (for example $x + y \le 4$ with $3x + 2y \ge 18$) has no solution.
- **Infinitely many optima:** if $Z$ has the same best value at two adjacent corners, every point of the edge between them is optimal; the objective line is parallel to that edge.

questions.stem_md: An imagined orange-juice unit in Nagpur plans how many litres of two juices to bottle each day. In its linear programming model, the decision variables stand for

options.text_md: the quantities the manager is free to choose, here the litres of each juice
the fixed limits on machine time and fruit supply
the profit earned on each litre
the corner points of the feasible region

questions.solution_md: Decision variables are the unknown quantities to be decided. The limits are the constraints, the profit per litre gives the coefficients of the objective function, and corner points come only after the region is drawn.

questions.stem_md: A manager is told that a linear programming model "assumes proportionality". Which of these is therefore a genuine limitation of the method?

options.text_md: It ignores the constraints when the region is bounded
Profit and resource use are assumed to change in exact proportion to the quantities, which real costs may not do
It cannot be used when there are exactly two decision variables
It always gives an answer in fractions

questions.solution_md: Linear programming treats every relation as linear: doubling output doubles profit and resource use. Real situations with discounts or overtime break this. Two-variable problems are exactly the ones solved graphically, answers need not be fractional, and constraints are never ignored.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is a typical application area of linear programming?

options.text_md: Solving a quadratic equation for a break-even price
Drawing a histogram of exam marks
Choosing the cheapest mix of foods that still meets nutrient needs
Finding the rate at which a balloon's volume grows

questions.solution_md: The diet problem is a classic linear programming application. The other three are calculus, algebra and statistics tasks with no linear objective to optimise under constraints.

questions.stem_md: A school canteen in an imagined Imphal school wants the cheapest combination of two snacks that gives each child at least a fixed amount of protein and iron. This linear programming problem is of which type?

options.text_md: A transportation problem
A manufacturing problem
A problem with no constraints
A diet problem

questions.solution_md: Minimising the cost of foods subject to minimum nutrient requirements is a diet problem. A transportation problem moves goods from sources to destinations; a manufacturing problem decides how much of each product to make with limited resources.

questions.stem_md: A tailor in Agra has $24$ m of cloth for the day. Each kurta uses $2$ m and each shirt $1.5$ m. If she stitches $x$ kurtas and $y$ shirts, the cloth constraint is
questions.solution_md: Cloth used: $2x + 1.5y \le 24$; doubling both sides gives $4x + 3y \le 48$. Option (b) reverses the inequality and option (d) uses the wrong unit.

questions.stem_md: A poultry farmer near Namakkal mixes $x$ kg of feed X and $y$ kg of feed Y. Each kilogram of X gives $3$ units of calcium and each kilogram of Y gives $1$ unit; the flock needs at least $12$ units a day. The calcium constraint is

options.text_md: $3x + y \ge 4$

questions.solution_md: Calcium supplied is $3x + 1 \cdot y$ and it must be **at least** $12$: $3x + y \ge 12$. Option (d) swaps the coefficients.

questions.stem_md: A stall's plan must satisfy $x + y \le 9$, $x + 3y \le 15$, $x \ge 0$, $y \ge 0$. Which of these plans is feasible?
questions.solution_md: $(6, 3)$: $9 \le 9$ and $15 \le 15$, so it is feasible (a corner). $(7, 3)$ and $(9, 1)$ give $x + y = 10$; $(2, 5)$ gives $x + 3y = 17$.

questions.stem_md: The four-sided region cut out by $x + y \le 9$, $x + 3y \le 15$ and the axes has four vertices. Which listed point is **not** one of them?
questions.solution_md: $(0, 9)$ is on $x + y = 9$ but gives $x + 3y = 27 > 15$, so it is not even feasible. The vertices are $(0, 0)$, $(9, 0)$, $(6, 3)$ and $(0, 5)$.

questions.stem_md: On the region with vertices $(0, 0)$, $(9, 0)$, $(6, 3)$, $(0, 5)$, a kiosk's earnings $Z = 4x + 5y$ (in ₹ hundred) are to be as large as possible. The greatest value is
questions.solution_md: Corner values: $0$, $36$, $24 + 15 = 39$, $25$. The greatest is $39$ at $(6, 3)$. Option (d) uses $(0, 9)$, which is not feasible.

questions.stem_md: The "at least" conditions $x + y \ge 8$ and $x + 3y \ge 12$, with $x, y \ge 0$, describe a region in the first quadrant. That region is

options.text_md: a single point
unbounded
a bounded quadrilateral
empty

questions.solution_md: Every point far enough from the origin, for example $(50, 50)$, satisfies both, so the region extends without limit: it is unbounded, with corners $(0, 8)$, $(6, 2)$ and $(12, 0)$.

questions.stem_md: A fertiliser blend must satisfy $x + y \ge 8$ and $x + 3y \ge 12$ ($x, y \ge 0$), giving corners $(0, 8)$, $(6, 2)$, $(12, 0)$ of an unbounded region. The least cost $Z = 3x + 5y$ is

options.text_md: not attained, because the region is unbounded

questions.solution_md: Corner values: $40$, $28$, $36$. The smallest is $28$. The open half-plane $3x + 5y < 28$ has no point in common with the region, so the minimum $28$ is attained at $(6, 2)$.

questions.stem_md: On the same unbounded region ($x + y \ge 8$, $x + 3y \ge 12$, $x, y \ge 0$), a student is asked for the **maximum** of $Z = x + 2y$. The correct conclusion is that the maximum

options.text_md: does not exist

questions.solution_md: The corner values are $16$, $10$, $12$, but the region is unbounded and the point $(0, 20)$ gives $Z = 40 > 16$. The half-plane $x + 2y > 16$ meets the region, so no maximum exists.

questions.stem_md: A courier van can carry at most $4$ crates ($x + y \le 4$), but the contract asks for a load worth at least $18$ units, $3x + 2y \ge 18$ ($x, y \ge 0$). What can be said about these constraints?

options.text_md: No load satisfies them: the feasible region is empty
The feasible region is unbounded
The only feasible load is $(4, 0)$
The feasible region is a triangle

questions.solution_md: With $x + y \le 4$, the largest value of $3x + 2y$ is $12$ (at $(4, 0)$), short of $18$. No point satisfies both constraints, so the problem is infeasible; even $(4, 0)$ gives only $12$.

questions.stem_md: A handloom unit's plan is limited by $x + y \le 12$, $2x + y \le 20$ and $x + 3y \le 30$ ($x, y \ge 0$). How many vertices does its feasible region have?
questions.solution_md: The vertices are $(0, 0)$, $(10, 0)$, $(8, 4)$, $(3, 9)$ and $(0, 10)$: a pentagon. With three non-trivial constraints the region can have up to five corners.

questions.stem_md: For the pentagon with vertices $(0, 0)$, $(10, 0)$, $(8, 4)$, $(3, 9)$, $(0, 10)$, the largest value of $Z = 2x + 5y$ is
questions.solution_md: Corner values: $0$, $20$, $36$, $6 + 45 = 51$, $50$. The largest is $51$ at $(3, 9)$, just above $50$ at $(0, 10)$.

questions.stem_md: On that pentagon (vertices $(0, 0)$, $(10, 0)$, $(8, 4)$, $(3, 9)$, $(0, 10)$), the total number of items $Z = x + y$ is maximised. How many optimal plans are there?

options.text_md: exactly one
exactly two
none
infinitely many

questions.solution_md: $Z(8, 4) = Z(3, 9) = 12$, larger than at the other corners, so every point of the edge joining them (the line $x + y = 12$) is optimal: infinitely many plans.

questions.stem_md: In a dairy's model, the pasteuriser line $2x + y = 14$ and the packing line $x + 2y = 13$ meet at a vertex of the feasible region. That vertex is
questions.solution_md: Double the second equation and subtract the first: $3y = 12$, $y = 4$; then $x = 13 - 8 = 5$. Check: $10 + 4 = 14$.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Anand dairy makes $x$ batches of paneer and $y$ batches of curd subject to $2x + y \le 14$ and $x + 2y \le 13$. The profit is ₹$30$ per paneer batch and ₹$40$ per curd batch (in hundreds). Its greatest profit, in ₹ hundred, is
A hostel mess requires $3x + 4y \ge 24$ units of energy from two dishes. Testing the origin for this constraint, the student should

options.text_md: pick another test point, since the origin lies on the line
note that the test is true and shade the side containing the origin
note that $0 \ge 24$ is false and shade the side of the line away from the origin
note that $0 \ge 24$ is false and shade the side containing the origin

questions.solution_md: At $(0, 0)$, $3x + 4y = 0$, which is not at least $24$. The origin is outside, so the feasible side of $3x + 4y = 24$ is the side away from it.

questions.stem_md: A mixed set of constraints, $x + 2y \ge 6$, $x + y \le 8$, $x \le 6$ ($x, y \ge 0$), gives a bounded region with vertices $(6, 0)$, $(6, 2)$, $(0, 8)$, $(0, 3)$. The maximum of $Z = 3x + 2y$ on it is
questions.solution_md: Corner values: $18$, $18 + 4 = 22$, $16$, $6$. The maximum is $22$ at $(6, 2)$.

questions.stem_md: A nutrition plan must meet $2x + y \ge 10$, $x + y \ge 7$ and $x + 2y \ge 10$ ($x, y \ge 0$); its vertices are $(0, 10)$, $(3, 4)$, $(4, 3)$, $(10, 0)$. The least value of $Z = 2x + 3y$ is
questions.solution_md: Corner values: $30$, $18$, $17$, $20$. The smallest is $17$; the half-plane $2x + 3y < 17$ contains no feasible point, so the minimum is $17$ at $(4, 3)$.

questions.stem_md: The fundamental result behind the corner point method says that when the feasible region is bounded and non-empty, a linear objective function

options.text_md: may have neither a maximum nor a minimum
has both a maximum and a minimum, and each occurs at a corner point
has a maximum but possibly no minimum
reaches its optimum only at an interior point

questions.solution_md: On a bounded, non-empty feasible region a linear $Z = ax + by$ attains both its maximum and its minimum, and each occurs at a corner point (possibly at two adjacent corners and the edge between them).

questions.stem_md: Depot P near Satna holds $100$ t of cement and sends $x$ t to site A and $y$ t to site B; the rest goes to site C. The amount sent from P to C is
questions.solution_md: Everything P holds is sent out, so $x + y + (\text{P to C}) = 100$, giving $100 - x - y$; it must be non-negative, which is the constraint $x + y \le 100$.

questions.stem_md: Which one of the following sets of conditions (each with $x \ge 0$, $y \ge 0$) gives a **bounded** feasible region?

options.text_md: $x + y \ge 5$
$x - y \le 2$
$y \ge 1$
$x + y \le 5$

questions.solution_md: $x + y \le 5$ keeps every point inside the triangle with vertices $(0, 0)$, $(5, 0)$, $(0, 5)$. Each of the others contains points such as $(100, 100)$ or $(0, 100)$, so those regions are unbounded.

questions.stem_md:

**Reason (R):** On a bounded feasible region, the maximum of a linear objective function occurs at a corner point.

Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

questions.solution_md: Corner values $0$, $21$, $23$, $13$ give the maximum $23$ at $(5, 4)$. R is the corner point result that justifies checking only the corners, so it explains A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The region $x + y \ge 8$, $x + 3y \ge 12$, $x, y \ge 0$ is unbounded.

**Reason (R):** A region described only by "$\ge$" constraints with positive coefficients is always bounded.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: $(40, 40)$ is feasible and the region goes on without end. R is false; such constraints keep points **away** from the origin, which makes the region unbounded, as here.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The origin satisfies the minimum-load condition $3x + 2y \ge 18$.

**Reason (R):** A point is feasible only when it satisfies every constraint of the problem.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** On the region $x + 2y \ge 6$, $x + y \le 8$, $x \le 6$, $x, y \ge 0$, the minimum of $Z = 3x + 2y$ is attained at $(0, 3)$.

**Reason (R):** The point $(0, 3)$ lies on the line $x + 2y = 6$.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

questions.solution_md: Corner values: $(6, 0) \to 18$, $(6, 2) \to 22$, $(0, 8) \to 16$, $(0, 3) \to 6$; the minimum $6$ is at $(0, 3)$, so A is true. R is true as well ($0 + 6 = 6$), but $(6, 0)$ also lies on that line and is not optimal, so R does not explain A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** For the canteen constraints $2x + y \ge 10$, $x + y \ge 7$, $x + 2y \ge 10$, $x, y \ge 0$, the least value $28$ of $Z = 4x + 4y$ is attained at infinitely many points.

**Reason (R):** If a linear objective takes the same optimal value at two adjacent corners, it takes that value at every point of the edge joining them.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

questions.solution_md: $Z(3, 4) = Z(4, 3) = 28$, while $Z(0, 10) = Z(10, 0) = 40$, and $4x + 4y < 28$ (that is, $x + y < 7$) breaks a constraint. So the minimum $28$ holds on the whole edge from $(3, 4)$ to $(4, 3)$: R explains A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A canteen's linear programming model may include the condition $x \le 30$ for the number of plates of one dish.

**Reason (R):** In a linear programming problem every constraint must be written as an equation.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: $x \le 30$ is a linear inequality, a perfectly good constraint. R is false: constraints are usually inequalities; only their boundary lines are equations.

questions.stem_md: In the graphical method, the decision variables of a linear programming problem may take only whole-number values.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Linear programming assumes divisibility: the variables may take any non-negative real values, and the optimum may be a fraction such as $(0, 6.5)$. Whole-number answers need extra conditions (or sensible rounding).

questions.stem_md: For the nutrition constraints $2x + y \ge 10$, $x + y \ge 7$, $x + 2y \ge 10$ ($x, y \ge 0$), the plan $(4, 3)$ is feasible.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True: $8 + 3 = 11 \ge 10$, $4 + 3 = 7 \ge 7$ and $4 + 6 = 10 \ge 10$; it is in fact a corner of the region.

questions.stem_md: If the feasible region of a linear programming problem is unbounded, the objective function can never have a minimum on it.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. On the unbounded region $x + y \ge 8$, $x + 3y \ge 12$, $x, y \ge 0$, the cost $Z = 3x + 5y$ has the minimum $28$ at $(6, 2)$; the half-plane test confirms it.

questions.stem_md: On the quadrilateral with vertices $(0, 0)$, $(9, 0)$, $(6, 3)$, $(0, 5)$, the function $Z = 2x + 7y$ is greatest at $(6, 3)$.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. $Z(6, 3) = 33$, but $Z(0, 5) = 35$ is the greatest of the corner values $0$, $18$, $33$, $35$.

questions.stem_md: The conditions $x \ge 0$ and $y \ge 0$, which say that the quantities produced or bought cannot be negative, are called the ____ constraints.
questions.solution_md: They are the non-negativity constraints.

questions.solution_md: Subtracting, $2y = 18$, so $y = 9$ (and $x = 3$).

questions.solution_md: Corner values $0$, $9$, $15$, $15$: the maximum is $15$, reached at two corners and along the edge between them.

questions.stem_md: A feasible solution at which the objective function takes its best value (largest for a maximum, smallest for a minimum) is called an ____ solution.
questions.solution_md: It is an optimal (optimum) feasible solution.

questions.solution_md: Corners $(0, 10)$, $(3, 4)$, $(4, 3)$, $(10, 0)$ give ₹$40$, ₹$31$, ₹$32$, ₹$50$. The half-plane $5x + 4y < 31$ has no feasible point, so the least cost is ₹$31$.

questions.stem_md: Using an imagined bakery that makes two kinds of biscuits, explain what is meant by (i) the objective function and (ii) the feasible region of a linear programming problem.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The **objective function** is the linear expression to be maximised or minimised, for example the bakery's profit $Z = 20x + 15y$ for $x$ trays of one biscuit and $y$ of the other.

(ii) The **feasible region** is the set of all points $(x, y)$ that satisfy every constraint (oven time, flour, $x, y \ge 0$) at the same time; only these plans can be carried out.

questions.solution_md: One definition each, with the context.

questions.stem_md: A cooperative in an imagined Kutch village asks whether linear programming is worth learning. State two advantages of the method for planning its production.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It gives the **best** (optimal) use of limited resources such as labour, machines and money, instead of a guess.

2. It makes the decision **systematic and clear**: all limits are written down, the effect of changing one of them can be studied, and bottlenecks become visible.

questions.solution_md: Any two genuine advantages.

questions.stem_md: A jeweller in an imagined Jaipur workshop makes $x$ rings and $y$ bangles a day. A ring takes $3$ hours and a bangle $2$ hours, and at most $24$ hours are available; at least $2$ rings must be made. Profit is ₹$400$ per ring and ₹$300$ per bangle. Formulate the linear programming problem.

answer.model_answer_md:
Maximise $Z = 400x + 300y$

Subject to $3x + 2y \le 24$ (hours), $x \ge 2$ (rings), and $y \ge 0$.

questions.solution_md: Objective, the hours constraint, the minimum-rings constraint and non-negativity.

questions.stem_md: For the dairy constraints $2x + y \le 14$, $x + 2y \le 13$, $x, y \ge 0$, decide whether the plans $P(3, 2)$ and $Q(6, 3)$ are feasible, giving reasons.

answer.model_answer_md:
$P(3, 2)$: $6 + 2 = 8 \le 14$ and $3 + 4 = 7 \le 13$, so $P$ is **feasible**.

$Q(6, 3)$: $12 + 3 = 15 > 14$, so the first constraint fails and $Q$ is **not feasible**.

questions.solution_md: Substitute each plan into both constraints.

questions.stem_md: Two boundaries of the canteen's nutrient region are $x + y = 7$ and $x + 2y = 10$. Find the vertex where they meet and check that it satisfies the third condition $2x + y \ge 10$.

answer.model_answer_md:
Subtract: $y = 3$, so $x = 4$. The vertex is $(4, 3)$.

Check: $2 \cdot 4 + 3 = 11 \ge 10$, so it is a corner of the region.

questions.solution_md: Eliminate x by subtraction, then test the third condition.

questions.stem_md: A region has vertices $(6, 0)$, $(6, 2)$, $(0, 8)$ and $(0, 3)$. Find the greatest and least values of $Z = 3x + 2y$ on it.
questions.solution_md: Evaluate Z at all four corners.

questions.stem_md: On the unbounded region $x + y \ge 8$, $x + 3y \ge 12$, $x, y \ge 0$ (vertices $(0, 8)$, $(6, 2)$, $(12, 0)$), show that the minimum of $Z = x + y$ is attained at infinitely many points.

answer.model_answer_md:
$Z(0, 8) = 8$, $Z(6, 2) = 8$, $Z(12, 0) = 12$. The half-plane $x + y < 8$ breaks the first constraint, so no feasible point does better: the minimum is $8$.

It occurs at the adjacent corners $(0, 8)$ and $(6, 2)$, hence at every point of the edge joining them: infinitely many points.

questions.solution_md: Equal values at two adjacent corners plus the half-plane check.

questions.stem_md: A courier van's constraints are $x + y \le 4$ and $3x + 2y \ge 18$ with $x, y \ge 0$. Show that the problem has no feasible solution.

answer.model_answer_md:
On $x + y \le 4$ (first quadrant) the corners are $(0, 0)$, $(4, 0)$, $(0, 4)$, where $3x + 2y$ is $0$, $12$, $8$; so $3x + 2y \le 12$ everywhere on that triangle.

Since $12 < 18$, no point meets both conditions: the feasible region is empty.

questions.solution_md: Largest value of 3x + 2y on the first triangle is 12.

questions.stem_md: For the unbounded region $x + y \ge 8$, $x + 3y \ge 12$, $x, y \ge 0$, show that $Z = x - y$ has no minimum value.

answer.model_answer_md:
Corner values: $Z(0, 8) = -8$, $Z(6, 2) = 4$, $Z(12, 0) = 12$; the smallest is $-8$.

But $(0, 9)$ is feasible ($9 \ge 8$, $27 \ge 12$) and gives $Z = -9 < -8$; moving up the $y$-axis makes $Z$ as small as we like, so no minimum exists.

questions.solution_md: A feasible point beats the best corner, so the half-plane x − y < −8 meets the region.

questions.stem_md: A kiosk's plan obeys $x + y \le 9$, $x + 3y \le 15$, $x, y \ge 0$. Using the graphical method, find the maximum of its takings $Z = 4x + 5y$ (in ₹ hundred) and the plan that gives it.

answer.model_answer_md:
Boundary lines: $x + y = 9$ through $(9, 0)$, $(0, 9)$; $x + 3y = 15$ through $(15, 0)$, $(0, 5)$. They meet where $2y = 6$: $(6, 3)$.

The feasible region is the quadrilateral with corners $(0, 0)$, $(9, 0)$, $(6, 3)$, $(0, 5)$.

$Z$: $0$, $36$, $39$, $25$. Maximum $39$ at $(6, 3)$.

questions.solution_md: Corners from the intersection, then Z at each corner.

questions.stem_md: For the handloom constraints $x + y \le 12$, $2x + y \le 20$, $x + 3y \le 30$, $x, y \ge 0$, find the corners of the feasible region and the maximum of $Z = 5x + 3y$.
questions.solution_md: Five corners, then evaluate Z.

questions.stem_md: Minimise $Z = 5x + 4y$ subject to $2x + y \ge 10$, $x + y \ge 7$, $x + 2y \ge 10$, $x, y \ge 0$, explaining why the answer is a true minimum although the region is unbounded.

answer.model_answer_md:
Corners: $(0, 10)$, $(3, 4)$, $(4, 3)$, $(10, 0)$ with $Z = 40, 31, 32, 50$. The smallest corner value is $31$ at $(3, 4)$.

Because the region is unbounded, draw the open half-plane $5x + 4y < 31$: it lies entirely below the line through $(3, 4)$ and has no point in common with the region.

Hence the minimum is $31$ at $(3, 4)$.

questions.solution_md: Corner values plus the half-plane test.

questions.stem_md: The Imphal canteen mixes $x$ packets of a millet snack and $y$ packets of a pulse snack. A millet packet gives $2$ units of protein, $1$ unit of iron and $1$ unit of fibre; a pulse packet gives $1$ unit of protein, $1$ unit of iron and $2$ units of fibre. Each class needs at least $10$ units of protein, $7$ of iron and $10$ of fibre. Packets cost ₹$5$ and ₹$4$. Formulate the linear programming problem.

answer.model_answer_md:
Minimise $Z = 5x + 4y$

Subject to $2x + y \ge 10$ (protein), $x + y \ge 7$ (iron), $x + 2y \ge 10$ (fibre), $x \ge 0$, $y \ge 0$.

questions.solution_md: One constraint per nutrient, an objective for cost.

questions.stem_md: On the handloom pentagon with vertices $(0, 0)$, $(10, 0)$, $(8, 4)$, $(3, 9)$, $(0, 10)$, the total number of pieces $Z = x + y$ is to be as large as possible. Find the maximum and describe all the optimal plans.

answer.model_answer_md:
$Z = 0, 10, 12, 12, 10$ at the corners. The maximum is $12$, at both $(8, 4)$ and $(3, 9)$.

These corners are adjacent, so $Z = 12$ at every point of the edge joining them, the part of $x + y = 12$ with $3 \le x \le 8$; for example $(5.5, 6.5)$.

There are infinitely many optimal plans.

questions.solution_md: Equal maximum at two adjacent corners.

questions.stem_md: For the bounded region $x + 2y \ge 6$, $x + y \le 8$, $x \le 6$, $x, y \ge 0$, find both the maximum and the minimum of $Z = x + 4y$.
questions.solution_md: Four corners, evaluate Z.

questions.stem_md: Describe the feasible region of the handloom constraints $x + y \le 12$, $2x + y \le 20$, $x + 3y \le 30$, $x, y \ge 0$: say which constraint bounds it on each stretch, and list its vertices.

answer.model_answer_md:
Along the $x$-axis it runs from $(0, 0)$ to $(10, 0)$, where $2x + y = 20$ cuts the axis.

From $(10, 0)$ to $(8, 4)$ the boundary is $2x + y = 20$; from $(8, 4)$ to $(3, 9)$ it is $x + y = 12$; from $(3, 9)$ to $(0, 10)$ it is $x + 3y = 30$; then down the $y$-axis.

Vertices: $(0, 0)$, $(10, 0)$, $(8, 4)$, $(3, 9)$, $(0, 10)$.

questions.solution_md: Each constraint is the boundary on one stretch.

questions.stem_md: On the unbounded region $x + y \ge 8$, $x + 3y \ge 12$, $x, y \ge 0$, find the minimum of $Z = 2x + y$, and decide whether $Z$ has a maximum there.

answer.model_answer_md:
Corners $(0, 8)$, $(6, 2)$, $(12, 0)$ give $Z = 8, 14, 24$. The half-plane $2x + y < 8$ contains no feasible point, so the minimum is $8$ at $(0, 8)$.

For a maximum: $(30, 0)$ is feasible and gives $60 > 24$; $Z$ grows without limit along the $x$-axis, so there is **no maximum**.

questions.solution_md: Half-plane test for the minimum; a far feasible point rules out a maximum.

questions.stem_md: State three limitations of linear programming that a planner at an imagined Hosur factory should keep in mind.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Linearity:** it assumes profit and resource use change in proportion to output, ignoring discounts, overtime rates and similar effects.

2. **Certainty:** all coefficients (prices, hours, availability) must be known exactly in advance.

3. **Single objective:** it optimises one quantity at a time, though real decisions may involve several goals; and fractional answers may need rounding when items are whole units.

questions.solution_md: Any three genuine limitations.

questions.stem_md: Depots P (holding $100$ t) and Q (holding $140$ t) near Satna supply sites A, B, C needing $50$ t, $70$ t and $120$ t. Let P send $x$ t to A and $y$ t to B. Express the other four shipments in $x$ and $y$, and write the constraints that make every shipment non-negative.

answer.model_answer_md:
P to C: $100 - x - y$. Q to A: $50 - x$. Q to B: $70 - y$. Q to C: $120 - (100 - x - y) = 20 + x + y$.

Non-negative shipments: $x \ge 0$, $y \ge 0$, $x \le 50$, $y \le 70$, $x + y \le 100$ (and $20 + x + y \ge 0$ holds automatically).

questions.solution_md: Use supplies and demands to express each route.

questions.stem_md:
A spice packer must satisfy $x + 2y \ge 6$ (minimum weight), $x + y \le 8$ (packets per hour) and $x \le 6$ (supply of one spice), with $x, y \ge 0$.

(a) Describe the feasible region and find its corner points. [2]

(b) Find the maximum and the minimum of $Z = 3x + 2y$ on it, stating where each occurs. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The region lies above $x + 2y = 6$, below $x + y = 8$ and to the left of $x = 6$. It is bounded, with corners $(6, 0)$, $(6, 2)$, $(0, 8)$, $(0, 3)$.

**(b)** $Z(6, 0) = 18$, $Z(6, 2) = 22$, $Z(0, 8) = 16$, $Z(0, 3) = 6$.

Maximum $22$ at $(6, 2)$; minimum $6$ at $(0, 3)$.

questions.stem_md:
A fertiliser blend must meet $x + y \ge 8$ and $x + 3y \ge 12$, $x, y \ge 0$.

(a) Find the minimum cost $Z = 3x + 5y$, explaining carefully why the corner value is a true minimum. [3]

(b) A trader suggests minimising $W = x - y$ instead. Decide whether $W$ has a minimum on this region and justify your answer. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Corners $(0, 8)$, $(6, 2)$, $(12, 0)$ give $Z = 40$, $28$, $36$. The region is unbounded, so test the open half-plane $3x + 5y < 28$: it lies on the origin side of the line through $(6, 2)$ and contains no feasible point. Hence the minimum cost is $28$ at $(6, 2)$.

**(b)** Corner values of $W$: $-8$, $4$, $12$. But $(0, 9)$ is feasible and gives $W = -9 < -8$; going further up the $y$-axis makes $W$ as small as we like. So $W$ has **no minimum**: an unbounded region need not have an optimum.

questions.solution_md: Half-plane test in (a); a counter-point in (b).
